newsitem.title: UK: UK trend to higher IT spending, more outsourcing.
newsitem.headline: UK trend to higher IT spending, more outsourcing.

text.p: Spending on information technology (IT) by investment firms in London's City is set to grow by a compounded annual growth rate of 10 percent up to 2000 and reveal a strong trend to outsourcing, a report from British-based management consultancy Datamonitor shows.

"Outsourcing, the millenium problem and single European currency issues...will result in a rise in total IT spend, most of which will be attributable to external (ex-company) suppliers," the report said.
The current estimated total IT bill for the City is around 2.6 billion stg, but is expected to grow 10.1 percent over the next five years to reach 4.2 billion stg in 2001.

The report splits the bill into internal, worth 44 percent of the total and external, worth 56 percent. Internal includes staff and maintenance while external spend comprises professional services, outsourcing, systems integration, hardware and software costs.
Datamonitor estimates that by 2001, internal spend will account for 36 percent of the total or 1.51 billion stg and external for 64 percent or 2.68 billion stg.

Currently, 40 percent of City firms' IT budget goes on front office functions and 36 percent on the back office. But this will change as back and middle offices become more automated and other functions are farmed out.
Changing demands will lead to a shake up in the industry with IT firms forming strategic alliances or acquiring small niche players in order to target their markets, the report said.
Low economic growth, low inflation and low interest rates are forcing City financial institutions to review their costs structures, market shares and products to find other ways of generating income.
IT directors polled said the main reasons for an IT review were the desire for better risk management, customer requirements or inability to handle current operations.

Other drivers were changes in regulation and the millenium issue -- where many computer sustems will have to be re-programmed to accept the year "2000" -- and the prospect of a single European currency.

Datamonitor also warned that City firms had realised that "investing in the latest technology does not necessarily sharpen competitive advantage". "IT systems need to be flexible, functionally rich, focused towards the end users and economically feasible," it said.
The main demands of IT systems from the users were a quality product or service, competitive cost, future adaptability, requirement sensitivity and "vertical market expertise".
Amongst systems already used, client/server technology has the highest importance, followed by network computing, object orientated technology, the Internet and Intranets.
